books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s (John L. Magee, 1856)

stimulus.source_note: Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s (John L. Magee, lithograph, 1856). Smithsonian, National Museum of American History (nmah_325684); Wikimedia Commons, File:Southern_Chivalry.jpg. Public domain.
stimulus.text: A lithograph published in 1856, titled “Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s.” It shows Representative Preston Brooks of South Carolina standing over Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts, who has fallen from his chair on the Senate floor, bleeding from the head and still holding a quill. Brooks raises his cane for another blow. In Sumner’s other hand is a paper marked “KANSAS.” Other members of Congress watch from behind, some smiling, some reaching out to stop the fight.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The cartoonist’s title, “Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s,” most directly suggests that

options.text: Sumner had challenged Brooks to settle the matter by duel.
options.misconception: No duel was offered or fought; Brooks struck Sumner as he sat at his Senate desk.

options.text: Southerners prized fair debate over brute force.
options.misconception: The cartoon shows the opposite: argument loses and the club wins, which is the cartoonist’s joke.

options.text: the Senate had voted to expel Brooks at once.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the House failed to expel Brooks, and he was re-elected by South Carolina.

options.text: Brooks answered words with violence, mocking the South’s code of honor.

rationales.A: No duel was offered or fought; Brooks struck Sumner as he sat at his Senate desk.
rationales.B: The cartoon shows the opposite: argument loses and the club wins, which is the cartoonist’s joke.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the House failed to expel Brooks, and he was re-elected by South Carolina.
rationales.D: The title sets “argument” against “club’s,” and the picture shows the club winning while Sumner lies bleeding.
rationales.general:
1. Read the title: “Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s” sets words against a weapon.
2. Look at the picture: Brooks swings his cane while Sumner lies bleeding at his desk.
3. Get the joke: a code of honor that answers a speech with a beating is no honor at all.
Remember: a cartoon’s title is its thesis; the picture is only the evidence.
